analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for the President or other officials to mislead Congress to win support for war.
analysis.headline: The Executive Accountability Act of 2009 was introduced by one senator, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, for the President, Vice President, or any executive branch official to knowingly lie or conceal material facts in order to talk Congress into authorizing military force. It would also pause the statute of limitations until the President's term ends, so a departing administration could still be prosecuted, and would require Congress to send any resolution finding a violation to the Attorney General. It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, whose elected representatives would vote on war based on honest information instead of statements that can't be criminally punished; and members of Congress, who would gain a legal tool to hold executive officials accountable for fabricated or misleading claims used to win votes for military force.

how_it_helps.text: It would make it a crime for the President, Vice President, or any executive branch official to knowingly and willfully falsify, conceal, or misstate material facts for the purpose of influencing Congress to authorize use of the armed forces, punishable by a fine and up to 10 years in prison [S2][S3].

The clock on prosecution would not start until the end of the President's term in office when the offense occurred, preventing an administration from running out the statute of limitations by leaving office [S2][S3].
If either chamber passed a resolution finding a violation, that resolution would have to be transmitted to the Attorney General for prosecution [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executive branch officials — the President, Vice President, and their staff — who would face criminal fines and up to 10 years' imprisonment if they misled Congress to gain support for military force.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement depends on Congress passing a resolution and the Attorney General — who serves in the same administration being accused — choosing to prosecute, so the bill's teeth depend on officials investigating their own boss [S2][S3].
The offense is narrow: it covers only statements made to win support for the use of military force, leaving misleading of Congress on other subjects unaddressed [S2][S3].

Critics of this kind of measure have generally argued it intrudes on the President's ability to give candid advice and to advocate for policy, and that existing laws already punish false statements to Congress — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge against a bill that never drew support to test the argument.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the public, the potential benefit is large: criminal accountability when the executive branch fabricates the case for war, with a limitations pause so an administration cannot simply outlast prosecution. The design is weaker than it looks — the Attorney General, who works for the accused president, holds the prosecutorial trigger — and the restriction on candid executive-Congress dealings is a real cost. On balance the bill's main weakness is not its design but its total lack of support: not even one cosponsor signed on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert C. Byrd (D-WV) introduced the Executive Accountability Act of 2009 in the Senate on July 28, 2009 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee [S5].
The bill's only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on July 30, 2009 [S5].
The Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill, and it never received a floor vote; the Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executive branch officials — the President, Vice President, and their staffs — who remain free of this specific criminal penalty for misleading Congress to build support for war. No one else gained.

for.name: Sen. Robert C. Byrd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on Sen. Byrd's behalf

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 28, 2009 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator is recorded as opposing; but with zero cosponsors, no one besides Sen. Byrd was recorded supporting it either.

industries.industry: Executive branch officeholders (President, Vice President, and executive branch employees)
industries.note: The bill would expose them to fines and up to 10 years in prison for lying to Congress to gain support for military force, and would pause the limitations clock until their term ends. Because it died, no such penalty exists.
